title: Black Smith Case Study
subtitle: Establishing a distribution center in Laval, Quebec.
html:
View full presentation · Canva ↗

Should the distribution center be owned?

This project evaluates whether Black Smith should establish a distribution center in Laval, Quebec. It compares three options: retaining fulfillment through Tempe, Arizona; using a third-party logistics provider (3PL) in Laval; and operating an owned distribution center. The decision is whether improvements in cost and service justify a new fixed investment.

The presentation recommends entering through a 3PL and deferring an owned facility. A better logistics route does not automatically justify committing to a warehouse, equipment, and staffing before demand can support their fixed costs.

Turning routes into a cost comparison

The model assumes 120,000 units annually, with 60% of demand in Canada and 40% in the United Kingdom. The existing network moves products from China through the Port of Los Angeles and Tempe before serving both markets. The alternative evaluates a configuration involving the Port of Montreal, Laval, and a 3PL.

The analysis compares unit costs, annual costs, tariffs, warehousing, and fulfillment charges. This prevents a lower cost on one transport leg from being mistaken for a more efficient network overall. It evaluates Laval 3PL feasibility through total logistics costs and the investment required to make the transition.

Balancing flexibility and control

A 3PL reduces upfront capital commitments, allows fulfillment spending to adjust with demand, and limits the need to manage warehouse staffing and compliance directly. The tradeoff is less control over service quality and operational changes. Customers still hold the brand responsible for delivery, even when another company fulfills the order.

An owned facility offers more direct control but requires enough sustained volume to absorb fixed costs. The project therefore evaluates payback, demand thresholds, implementation time, service performance, and tariff uncertainty together rather than comparing warehouse prices alone.

Why the decision matters

Facility location and ownership affect cost, cash commitments, service, and the ability to adapt. Testing the market through a 3PL creates an opportunity to observe actual demand and fulfillment performance before committing to an owned facility.

The project turns a broad expansion question into testable conditions: Does routing improve? Do total costs fall? Can service requirements be met? Does demand justify fixed investment? This connects facility decisions to operating efficiency, financial exposure, and room for future expansion.
